slides.title: Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data
slides.content:
Aditya Cowsik*, Kfir Dolev*, Michael Y. Li*, G. Bruno De Luca, Nourya Cohen, Noah D. Goodman, Yoav Levine (* equal contribution)
Independent Researcher · Tel Aviv University · Stanford University · LAPTh, USMB
arXiv:2609.30063v1, 24 Sep 2026
William Liaw · Lab meeting

"So much from so little, almost everything from almost nothing." (John Archibald Wheeler; epigraph, p.1)
slides.notes: Title, authors, affiliations and arXiv ID as printed on p.1. The footnote 'Equal contribution; authors listed alphabetically' is attached to the asterisks on Cowsik, Dolev and Li, who are in alphabetical order. The other four are not, so do not read credit into position. Both epigraphs are on p.1: Wheeler (here) and Seneca, 'By teaching, we learn.' (used on the self-play slide). Set scope up front: the Abstract calls this 'an initial proof-of-concept', and the experiments are 'confined to models below 25M parameters at a 4K context' (p.15). Code: the paper links no method code. Its only code link is a third-party forward-mode attention kernel (p.6, footnote 1). The authors' X thread links github.com/acowsik/self_play_pretraining, described as figures, tables and evaluation code, not a training release. I have not inspected it.

slides.title: Data is still largely curated on the model's behalf
slides.content:
- Pretraining is driven by "scaling pretraining on ever more data", yet the data is "still largely curated on the model's behalf" (Abstract)
- Curation today: data curation, data-mixture design, hand-designed synthetic generators (p.1)
- Proposal: let the model "learn to generate the data most useful for its own improvement" (Abstract)
- Setting: generator and learner both randomly initialized; all learner data comes from self-play (p.2)
- No natural data in any gradient update; natural validation loss (DCLM, DNA) chose hyperparameters (p.8)
- Scope: models below 25M params, 4K context (p.15); max budget 34.36B tokens (p.8); loss in bits per byte

Test: does zero-shot loss on natural data improve predictably with self-play compute? (Abstract)
slides.notes: Quotes: Abstract and Intro p.1, whose curation sentence cites Li 2025, Penedo 2023, Soldaini 2024; Chen 2026, Xie 2023; Gunasekar 2023, Yang 2025. The paper frames this as extending 'the Bitter Lesson [Sutton, 2019] to the training data itself' (p.1), and asks whether useful structure 'can emerge ex nihilo' (p.2). Scope of 'zero data', in the paper's words (p.8): 'This introduces limited leakage through hyperparameter selection, but natural data are never used for gradient updates.' So zero holds for gradients, not for selection or design. Design was also hand-chosen: the reward was picked 'after searching through several possibilities at small scale' (p.5), and the macros were kept after 'preliminary experiments' (App. E, p.30). The critique section returns to all three. The bottom line is the paper's own test, which Results answers.

slides.title: Roadmap
slides.content:
Background (Solomonoff, self-play) -> Method (machine, models, reward, loop) -> Results (scaling, exponents, generator, ICL, warm start, ablations) -> Critique and discussion
Question pauses after Method and after Results; open discussion at the end
slides.notes: About 15 seconds. Two short pauses: after Method (about 1.5 min) and after Results (about 1.5 min). The open discussion at the end runs about 18 minutes on the final slide. Keep the paper's test from the previous slide in mind: Results answers it, and the critique checks how well.

slides.title: Solomonoff induction: the idealized target
slides.content:
Background, not this paper (Solomonoff 1964a, as restated in Grau-Moya et al. 2024, Sec. 1, p.3):
M(x) = sum over programs p with U(p) = x* of 2^(-l(p))
(U a monotone universal machine; x* any output starting with x; the whole program p is read)

- Hypothesis class: all computable data-generating processes, with unbounded compute (p.2)
- Uncomputable; the paper aims at "an efficient computable approximation to universal prediction" (p.2)
- Paper's generator prior (p.6): g_0(x) = |A|^(-l(x)), l = tokens through F, "the natural analog of the Solomonoff prior 2^(-|p|)"
- Hypothesized regularities self-play should find: "copying, recursion, and hierarchical composition" (p.2)
slides.notes: Background only. The paper cites the prior 2^(-|p|) (Solomonoff 1964; p.6), not the mixture M. Definition from Grau-Moya et al. 2024, Def. 2 (arXiv 2401.14953, p.3). If asked about guarantees: Solomonoff (1964a), restated there, bounds the summed expected squared error, sum_t sum_{x<t} mu(x<t) sum_x (M - mu)^2 <= K(mu) ln 2, where K(mu) = min{l(p): U(p) = mu} is the length of the shortest program computing the true source mu. The paper uses the prior twice: as the KL anchor g_0 (Eq. 3, p.6) and as the baseline sampler, tokens 'drawn i.i.d. until termination, giving full support to every finite program while favoring shorter descriptions' (p.8). |A| is ambiguous: App. E lists 9 base symbols, while generation uses 19 tokens (Sec. 2.3). [mine] Program space plays the role of the hypothesis class, and self-play is a finite-compute search over it. Grau-Moya's Thm. 9 says non-uniform program samplers keep universality under conditions; this paper never invokes it.

slides.title: Self-play: search where the learner can still learn
slides.content:
- The program space is enormous, and "whether a sequence is useful changes as the learner improves" (p.2)
- So the generator adapts: RL toward programs "near the frontier of the learner's current capabilities" (p.2)
- Rejected reward, difficulty: "a program can be made arbitrarily difficult without containing useful structure", e.g. by injecting random bytes (p.5)
- Used instead: reward programs whose learner gradients align with the learner's own parameter movement (Eq. 2, in Method)
- Reward chosen by search at small scale (p.5); ablated at 1M params (Table 5, p.31)

"By teaching, we learn." (Seneca; epigraph, p.1)
slides.notes: No equations here; the loop diagram and Eq. 2 come next in Method. The difficulty reward was 'motivated by prior work on self-play [Bailey et al., 2026a, Dong and Ma, 2025b]' (p.5). Bailey et al. report a conjecturer that collapses to 'artificially complex problems' (arXiv 2604.20209), the same failure mode. [interp] Lineage: Schmidhuber's compression progress (2008) and PowerPlay (2012) are cited (p.13). Graves et al. 2017 (learning-progress bandits) and PAIRED (regret instead of difficulty) are close but uncited. Exact p.5 wording: 'we selected this reward after searching through several possibilities at small scale.' The matched control is in the body text (p.8): both methods use 'exactly the same program space' and 'differ only in whether the sampling distribution adapts to the learner.' Hedge: the paper calls discovered structure 'one mechanism driving the faster scaling' (p.9), and the self-play arm also has replay and mutation pools that Fig. 2 does not ablate.

slides.title: The loop: generator writes programs, learner predicts bytes
slides.content:
Two random-init Llama decoders, same architecture, independent weights (pp.4, 7)
- Generator g_phi samples programs; machine U runs them into bytes; learner pi_theta predicts the bytes (Sec. 2, p.4)
- The learner trains on the output bytes, not on the programs (Sec. 2.1, p.4)
- The learner's own gradients score each program; that score is the generator's reward
- Generator update: policy gradient on the reward, plus reward-weighted SFT over a pool of fresh, replayed and mutated programs (p.4; Eq. 5)
- In the loop, no natural data in any gradient step; natural data enters only through validation-based selection (p.8) and zero-shot evaluation
- Downstream, the final self-play checkpoint also initializes natural-data pretraining (App. A.1)
slides.diagram: One row, left to right. Box A 'Generator g_phi' (sub-label 'Llama, random init'); small box under A 'pool: fresh + mutated + replay'. Arrow A->B labeled 'program x_i: variable length <= L, ends in F (sampled over 19 logits)'. Box B 'Universal machine U' (sub-label 'Brainf*ck + 10 macros'); small box 'random tape omega_i' with a downward arrow into B. Arrow B->C labeled 'bytes y_i = U(x_i, omega_i)'. Box C 'Learner pi_theta' (sub-label 'Llama, random init'); the incoming arrow also labeled 'next-byte cross-entropy (Eq. 1)'. Return arrow along the bottom from C to A labeled 'reward r_i (Eq. 2) -> policy gradient + reward-weighted SFT (Eqs. 3-5)'. Top right: dashed grey box 'Natural data: no gradient steps'; dashed arrow from C to it labeled 'zero-shot eval; val loss for hyperparameters, checkpoints, frontier (p.8)'. Caption: 'Adapted from Fig. 1 (top, p.3); arrows and labels are mine.'
slides.notes: Walk the loop once (Sec. 2 items 1-3, p.4). Both networks start random: 'tabula rasa' (p.2). The learner sees bytes: 'These output bytes, rather than the programs themselves, constitute the learner's training data' (p.4). Sec. 2 item 3 also gives the generator 'a supervised fine-tuning objective on existing programs to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and on mutated programs to promote exploration' (p.4). Natural data touches the self-play pipeline only through selection: DCLM + DNA validation loss picks hyperparameters, and each dataset's validation loss picks checkpoints, ensemble sizes and frontier points (p.8). Plus zero-shot evaluation. App. A.1 is separate: there, self-play checkpoints are warm starts that do train on natural data. 19 is the logit set (8 + 10 + F, p.7), not program length; programs are in A^{<=L} (p.4), and L is not reported. The paper's own diagram is figs/fig1a-method-diagram.png.

slides.title: Program language: Brainf*ck plus 10 hand-picked macros
slides.content:
- 8 Brainf*ck instructions < > + - [ ] . , plus end token F; Turing complete with the 8 alone (App. E, pp.29-30)
- Byte cells mod 256 on a circular tape; unmatched brackets are no-ops, so every string runs (App. E, p.30)
- ',' reads i.i.d. uniform bytes from a random tape omega (App. E, p.30), so one program is a distribution over outputs (Sec. 2.1, p.4)
- Output y = first T bytes emitted, zero-padded if the program halts early
- Example (deterministic, no ','): +++[>+.<-]F emits y = (1, 2, 3, 0, ..., 0) (App. E, p.30)
- 10 macros, shared by all methods and baselines (Table 4, p.30); four that appear in Table 1 programs:
Token | Expansion | Effect
C | [->+>+<<] | clear; add x into the two right cells
L | [->+++<] | clear; add 3x into right neighbor
V | [.>] | print stored string until a zero cell
X | [-] then 16 x + | set cell to 16
- Generator logits: 8 + 10 + F (Sec. 2.3, p.7); 19 total is my sum
slides.notes: App. E and Table 4 (pp.29-30). Macros are expansions into pure Brainf*ck, idioms 'frequently used in human written Brainf*ck programs' that 'appear to increase the efficiency of self-play in preliminary experiments' (p.30). The paper notes that all methods use the same augmented alphabet. Do not show the printed Table 4 crop: row C prints '[->+>+«]', a typo for '<<'. Other macros: Z [-], R [->+<], N [-<->], G [>], H [<], W [[-]>+<]. R also appears in the quadratic program. For randomness, Table 1's Fibonacci program S,[[.C>.C>] starts with ','. My re-implementation gives 1,1,2,3,5 only when the random byte is 1; otherwise r*(1,1,2,3,5,...) mod 256. So Table 1 outputs are one tape draw. Not reported: T, L, step budget, tape length. [mine] T is probably 4,095, since PCFG rows are 4,095 bytes (App. H) and the context is 4,096 with an O prefix. The crop shows the p.30 for-loop example.

slides.title: Generator and learner: same architecture, two objectives
slides.content:
Generator g_phi
- Llama decoder, random init; samples over 19 logits until F (Sec. 2.3, p.7)
- Prior g_0(x) = |A|^(-l(x)), the "fixed uniform program prior" (p.6); |A| = 19 is my reading (App. E's base alphabet has 9)
- Objective (Eq. 3): J(phi) = E_{x~g_phi}[r(x)] - beta * KL(g_phi || g_0); GRPO-style advantage over the round pool, plus expert iteration (Eqs. 4-5, p.6)
Learner pi_theta
- Same Llama architecture, independent init; byte vocabulary of 256 (Sec. 2.3)
- Next-byte cross-entropy on outputs y_i; per-program loss = mean over "content tokens"
- Pool loss (Eq. 1): (1/M_e) sum_{i in B_e} L(y_i; theta), equal weight per program; fresh, mutated and replay programs all train it (p.5)
Footer: tuned per scale by coordinate descent: learner LR, generator-to-learner LR ratio, batch size, beta (p.8); values not reported
slides.notes: Advantage (p.6): A_i = (r_i - mean_e r)/(std_e r + eps) - beta*(log g_phi(x_i) - log g_0(x_i)), normalized over the full round pool. Eq. 4: policy gradient with a sequence-level importance ratio clipped to [e^-20, e^20]. It is 1 for fresh samples; for replay, the denominator is the probability stored at bank entry. Mutants are excluded from L_PG because they 'were not sampled from a proposal distribution with a well-defined log probability'. They still enter L_EI. Expert iteration: weights w_i = [r_i]+ / sum [r_j]+ over the whole pool, lambda_EI = 1.0 (Eq. 5). [mine] [.]+ is a no-op since r >= 0. Generator 'initialized near g_0 and regularized toward it throughout' (p.6). 'Content tokens' is undefined: prefixes and zero padding may or may not count. Sizes: 1M (Table 5, Fig. 3), 24.4M (App. A.1), 'below 25M' (p.15). Crops: figs/eq3-rl-objective.png, figs/eq-advantage.png.

slides.title: The reward: alignment with the learner's own progress
slides.content:
Reward = how far a program's gradient points along the learner's preconditioned parameter movement over the lookback window

r_i = | < grad_theta L(y_i; theta_e), P_e (.) delta_theta_e > |   (Eq. 2, p.5)
delta_theta_e = theta_{floor(e/2)} - theta_e        P_e = lr / (sqrt(v_hat_e) + eps), the diagonal AdamW step operator

- Expected (p.5): mastered programs give near-zero gradients; unrelated or unlearnable ones do not align with the movement; both get little reward
- First order (my reading): roughly the loss decrease on y_i between theta_{floor(e/2)} and theta_e, unsigned and preconditioned
- Forward-mode autodiff, no full gradients (p.6); one JVP per program is my reading
- Lookback grows with training; reward chosen "after searching through several possibilities at small scale" (p.5)
- What each piece buys: Table 5, in Results
slides.notes: Eq. 2 is on p.5; typeset crop at figs/eq-generator-reward.png. Window: the text's 'lookback window of ceil(e/2)' is the length e - floor(e/2), so it agrees with Eq. 2's checkpoint theta_{floor(e/2)} and with Table 5's caption. The window 'helps average over short-term fluctuations' and 'allows early mistakes to eventually be forgotten' (p.5). [mine] First-order reading: <grad L(theta_e), theta_past - theta_e> ~ L(y; theta_past) - L(y; theta_e), with the gradient taken at theta_e. The paper calls its loss_delta variant 'putatively similar ... (to first order)' (p.31). At e = 0 the window is empty, so r = 0. The lr scalar cancels under the advantage's std normalization. Preconditioning 'was important in line with Thrush et al. [2026]' (p.5), but no Table 5 row removes it. The absolute value is defended on p.31, from 1M-param ablations with mixed evidence (Results). Whether theta_e and v_hat_e are read before or after round e's learner step is not stated.

slides.title: One self-play round, reconstructed
slides.content:
My reconstruction from Sec. 2 (p.4), Eqs. 1-5 and App. G; the paper has no algorithm box
for round e = 0, 1, ...:
  1 sample     programs from g_phi over 19 logits until F (length varies, <= L); store sampling probabilities
  2 pool       B_e = fresh (a fraction replaced by mutants) + mutated archive elites + replayed old programs on new tapes
  3 execute    y_i = U(x_i, omega_i)
  4 learner    one AdamW step on Eq. 1 over the whole pool
  5 generator  reward r_i (Eq. 2), then one step on L_PG + 1.0 * L_EI
  6 archive    positive-reward programs into MAP-Elites (<= 36 niches, top 8 each; stored rewards x 0.97 per round)

Not reported in the paper: N; mutation and replay fractions; bank size; T; L; step budget; learner LR; generator/learner LR ratio; beta; batch size; K
slides.notes: Round order follows the paper's list (p.4): one learner gradient step, then one generator step. Whether Eq. 2 reads theta_e and v_hat_e before or after that learner step is not stated. App. G (pp.31-32): mutation is a single-token substitution, insertion or deletion of an archived elite. Niches: max dynamic loop depth 0-8 (clamped) by body length bucketed at 8, 16 and 32 tokens, so at most 36. Only programs with positive reward enter, top 8 per niche, and stored rewards decay 0.97 per round. Parents are chosen uniformly over occupied niches. Replay draws uniformly without replacement from the bank of non-replay programs and re-runs them with fresh tapes. App. C counts '1,024 newly generated programs per round', 'the same rate' as the scaling experiments, but batch size was tuned (p.8). Programs were saved every 256 rounds. Whether mutants enter the replay bank is unstated; their importance-ratio denominator would be undefined.

slides.title: Compute and selection: what the scaling axis counts
slides.content:
- x-axis on Figs. 1, 2, 7: C = K x params x tokens; K = independent seeds ensembled (p.8; Fig. 1 label)
- Fixed max budget 34.36B tokens; short warmup then constant LR, so every checkpoint is a shorter run; context 4,096 (p.8)
- Frontier over model size, checkpoint and ensemble size: a point counts only if its validation loss beats every configuration with <= compute (p.8)
- Selection uses the reported validation loss: DCLM + DNA for tuning, each dataset's own validation loss for its frontier; no separate test split described (p.8)
- Fit per dataset: L(C) = E + A * C^(-alpha), bits/byte (p.8)
- No FLOPs or GPU-hours reported; C has no generator, JVP or execution term (my reading)
- My illustration, not the paper's: K = 8, N = 24.4M (the App. A.1 model; scaling models only "below 25M", p.15), D = 34.36B gives C ~ 6.7e18, near the right edge of Figs. 1-2; 6*N*D*K ~ 4e19 FLOPs
slides.notes: Sec. 3.1 (p.8). Ensembles average 'the models' predictive distributions'; whether probabilities or log-probabilities is unstated. Batch-size changes alter the number of rounds, not total tokens. With constant LR, the training duration is chosen retrospectively. The frontier is Kaplan-style (Kaplan et al. 2020). [mine] 34.36B = 2^35 = 8,192 rounds x 1,024 programs x 4,096 tokens. That fits App. C's 1,024 programs per round, but batch size was tuned, so the split is a guess. The paper reports K only for side experiments: 8 seeds in Fig. 3(a) (whose caption says four) and 4-seed ensembles in Table 5. So the illustration's K = 8 and N = 24.4M are my assumptions. Constant LR without decay is conservative on loss but may bias the exponent. The selection point matters for the critique: the reported zero-shot curves are best-over-configurations on the same validation data.

slides.title: Questions on the method?
slides.content:
Questions on the method?
If the room is quiet:
- Does the reward matter beyond the pool machinery (mutation, replay, expert iteration)? Table 5 answers part of this in Results
- Is the 19-token language a hand-built prior? Same alphabet for every method (App. E, p.30); macros kept after preliminary runs; X = 16 and mod-256 are unablated
- What should count as compute? C has no generator or JVP term
slides.notes: Pause for about 1.5 minutes. On Q1: the paper ablates only the reward (Table 5). Policy gradient, expert iteration, mutation, replay and the MAP-Elites archive are never ablated, and curriculum ablations are listed as future work (p.15). On Q2: App. E says the added primitives 'cannot account for any difference between self-play and its controls' because all methods share them (p.30). That is fair for relative claims, but not for absolute transfer. [mine] X = 16 and the mod-256 tape have no stated justification. On Q3: C = K x params x tokens counts the learner only, by my reading (Fig. 1 axis). Still unreported: |A| (9 vs 19), T, L, step budget, beta, N, the mutation and replay fractions, and the model-size list.

slides.title: Zero-shot eval: every dataset is a byte stream
slides.content:
- Metric: next-byte loss in bits/byte; uniform over 256 bytes = 8; DNA's 8-symbol alphabet floor = 3 (App. B.5, p.27)
- No gradient step on any eval dataset (p.8); DCLM and DNA also selected hyperparameters (see Method)
- Six byte encodings, each defined in App. B: text (UTF-8), images (CIFAR-10, HWC or planar), speech (PCM16 -> 1 byte per sample), melody (16th-note grid), DNA, code
- Record lengths differ: speech, Metamath, C: 255-byte records at context 256; DNA: 255-symbol records; melody: 255 bytes = 63.75 quarter notes (B.4), pieces truncated to 4,095 bytes; DCLM window not stated; CIFAR image = 3,072 bytes
- Training context: 4,096
slides.notes: Melody (B.4, Fig. 10 shown): 40 'highly recognizable' public-domain pieces from Mutopia, melody only, 16th-note grid. Codes: 0-127 pitch onset, 128 hold, 129 pause, 130 end, one note per cell. Beethoven's Fifth: 67,128,67,128,67,128,63, then seven 128s. Text (B.1): DCLM, UTF-8, fixed windows (Fig. 8). Images (B.2): CIFAR-10 test batch; planar CHW is described in B.2 text, while Fig. 9 shows HWC only. Speech (B.3): Speech Commands, floor((s+32768)/256); 255 bytes = 15.94/31.88/63.75 ms at 16/8/4 kHz. [mine] Encodings are hand-chosen, so bits/byte is not one common task. App. B documents 7 sources. Nine Fig. 7 datasets have no entry: Common Crawl, Kolmogorov text, GitHub Python, arXiv math, LibriSpeech, ESC-50, MusicNet, glibc rand, Arithmetic. MusicNet (Thickstun, Harchaoui and Kakade 2017) is in Fig. 2 but not in the references.

slides.title: Scaling: self-play vs. two fixed priors (Fig. 2)
slides.content:
Models < 25M params, 4,096-token context, 34.36B-token budget (pp.8, 15)
x: C = K x params x tokens (K = seeds ensembled; learner only, my reading) · y: bits/byte, both log
- Universal prior (same program space, tokens i.i.d. until F) "scales substantially more slowly" (Fig. 2, p.7)
- PCFG "stronger on text and code"; self-play "substantially outperforms it on images, music, audio, and speech" (p.9)
- Melody (Mutopia) is close to PCFG at matched compute (plot read)
- DCLM anchors (plot reads): self-play ~4.6 and PCFG ~3.7 near 4e17; universal prior ~6.9 near 1e17; self-play ~4.4 at ~1e18
- Fig. 7: same format on 21 datasets; glibc rand stays near 8 bits
slides.notes: Point at Images and Text first, then the rest. Fig. 2 (p.7) shows 8 of the 21 Fig. 7 panels (p.23). Caption: 'access to a universal space of programs alone is insufficient without the adaptive curriculum'; the frontier 'ends where we do not find further models with smaller loss'. Plot reads, approximate: CIFAR-10 self-play ~5.05 at ~6e18 (matches the HWC curve in Fig. 7) vs PCFG ~7.55 and universal prior ~7.4. LibriSpeech PCM8 ~2.1 vs PCFG ~5.0. MusicNet 44.1 kHz ~1.85 vs PCFG ~2.8. Melody: PCFG ~2.2 at ~4e17, with self-play ~2.0 there. [mine] At the largest compute, self-play points sit above the fitted line on DCLM, Python, C, Common Crawl, melody and audio, hinting at flattening; the fits are never tested out of sample. glibc rand is a negative control the text never discusses; Table 5's random-bytes row is 8.02. No natural-data baseline appears in Fig. 2.

slides.title: Exponents vs literature: a bit higher; DNA far above
slides.content:
Fit: L(C) = A * C^(-b) + E (Table 2, p.21); same exponent as alpha in Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 1
Paper: "broadly similar ... if a bit higher" (p.21); DNA "the exceptional case" (p.8)
Dataset | Ours b | Literature b
text (DCLM) | 0.123 | 0.048-0.099†
CIFAR-10 image bytes | 0.145 | 0.065†-0.10
audio 8-bit PCM | 0.260 | 0.12†-0.14†
DNA (8-symbol) | 0.435 | 0.01-0.06
Metamath set.mm | 0.129 | 0.17
C source (AITDCC) | 0.116 | 0.17†
- Higher in 4 of 6 (text 1.2-2.6x the range, 8-bit audio about 2x); lower on Metamath and C
- Same CIFAR-10 images: HWC 0.066 vs "image bytes" 0.145; B.2 reports "no appreciable effect" of byte order; the gap is unexplained
- Our fits: models < 25M params; literature rows: other models, tokenizers and data
† derived from Chinchilla-form fits, b = alpha*beta/(alpha+beta), under the compute-optimal allocation
slides.notes: Full table crop: figs/tab2-compute-exponents.png (10 rows). Rows with no literature value: CIFAR-10 HWC 0.066, audio 16-bit 0.141, MIDI 0.249, Python 0.113. Fig. 1 headlines Images 0.066 (the HWC row), Text 0.123 and Melody 0.249, a 3.8x spread (my calc). The audio rows name no dataset, and Table 2 never says the 'image bytes' row is planar, although Table 5 and Fig. 7 use 'planar'. Literature: text from Aghajanyan 2023 (0.048) and Henighan 2020 (0.099†); DNA from Shah et al. 2026. No E, A, confidence intervals or fit window are reported. [mine] DNA is also a hyperparameter-selection dataset (p.8). Sec. 4 links the self-play exponent (gamma*eta, Eq. 10) to natural-data exponents via beta_obs ~ min{beta*nu, gamma*mu} (Eq. 13). Equating them needs eta ~ mu, which is argued, not measured. The paper itself says to 'cautiously interpret' this (p.13).

slides.title: Math families appear early under self-play (Table 1)
slides.content:
Round = 1,024 programs (App. C, "the same rate" as the scaling runs)
- Arithmetic is not accelerated: round 0 vs ~105 under the universal prior
- Fibonacci, geometric, quadratic, cubic: all by round 512 under self-play
- Universal prior: 0 hits in 1.64e8 samples -> p <= 1.8e-8 (rule of three, one-sided 95%) -> first round > 53,000 (App. C, p.29)
- Self-play saved only every 256 rounds, so its rounds are upper bounds (App. C, p.28)
- Paper: "one mechanism driving the faster scaling" (p.9); causal link to transfer untested (p.15)
slides.notes: Table 1 is p.9; Table 3 (p.28) repeats it. The universal baseline is checked every round and self-play only every 256, so 'the comparison therefore underestimates the gap' (App. C). Arithmetic: 1,526 hits, p ~ 9.3e-6, first round ~105 (95% CI 100-111). The paper notes the zero-hit result 'establishes only a common lower bound on their rarity'. Detection (App. C): up to 30 unrelated leading bytes; the rest must satisfy the recurrence mod 256 (constant 1st/2nd/3rd differences; v_n = v_{n-1} + v_{n-2}; v_n = r*v_{n-1}); minimal period >= 30. Programs use macros C, L, R, V, X. [mine] Outputs shown for programs that read ',' are one tape draw (Fibonacci r = 1, quadratic r = 9, per my re-implementation). Not stated: how many self-play programs were searched, or what fraction of generator mass these families take. The families were named after observation.

slides.title: Later checkpoints: more structure, transfer flattens
slides.content:
Setup (p.9): for endpoint T, a corpus of 4.19M programs sampled across 16 generator snapshots ending at T; a fresh 1M-param learner trains one epoch on each
Epiplexity = "the excess training loss the learner accumulates before converging" (Fig. 3 caption); units nats x rounds
- (a) Epiplexity rises: ~15 at g0 -> ~1,700 at g4,096 (mean of 8); ~1,240 without the off-scale 5,001 seed (plot read, my calc)
- (b) Val BPB falls, then flattens (plot reads): text ~8.4 -> ~5.2 by g1,024, ~5.3 at g4,096; audio ~5.4 -> 5.2 after g512; images still falling slowly (~6.8 -> ~6.3)
- Paper: "Both improve steadily with T" (p.9)
slides.notes: Fig. 3, p.10; method on p.9. Epiplexity is from Finzi et al. 2026, 'the amount of structure extractable by a compute-bounded learner' (p.9). Seed counts conflict within the paper. The caption says 'four seeds per endpoint', while panel (a) says 'mean of 8 seeds'. Panel (b) says 'mean of 4-seed subsets, +/-1 SD over subsets', while the caption says '4 ensembled seeds'. Flag this as a question for the authors. [mine] The structure measure keeps rising while text and audio transfer saturate after g512 to g1,024. The text uptick at g4,096 is within the error bars. Each corpus mixes 16 snapshots, so this tests a mixture, not an ordering. It does not separate an adaptive curriculum from a good static distribution, and there is no early-only vs late-only control at equal corpus size. One learner size (1M) and one budget.

slides.title: ICL: self-play learns in context; fixed priors mostly don't
slides.content:
Format: m examples of [0, x1..xk, f(x)], then a query; greedy argmax exact match; no gradient updates (p.10; App. D, Eq. 14)
Chance: 1/256 ~ 0.004 for a uniform byte guess (dashed line; my calc). Y-axis is nonlinear
- Self-play: reverse string, stack, associative recall reach "almost 100%" after a sufficient number of examples (p.11)
- MAX and MIN at m = 0: text reports 6%-8% from a copying prior (p.11); the plot reads ~4-5%
- SUM at m = 0 is at chance
- Universal prior: "little evidence of effective ICL"; SUM at most ~1.5% (Fig. 4 caption; plot)
- PCFG: "performs strongly on associative recall but transfers only weakly to the remaining tasks" (Fig. 4 caption)
- Not stated: model scale (only "below 25M", p.15), dictionary size V, k, instance counts
slides.diagram: Overlay on the Fig. 4 crop: a dashed horizontal line at 0.004 in each of the three panels, labeled 'chance (1/256)'. Build in three steps: (1) the Self-play panel alone, with reverse string, stack and assoc called out; (2) add the Universal prior and PCFG panels; (3) highlight the PCFG assoc curve.
slides.notes: Fig. 4, p.10; the same tasks appear in Fig. 1 (lower right). Plot reads at the largest m: stack and reverse ~1.0, assoc ~0.9-1.0, SUM ~0.85, MAX and MIN ~0.65-0.7. Reverse and stack stop near m ~ 128. Also at m = 0 (plot reads, not discussed in the paper): self-play stack ~0.35; PCFG assoc ~0.6 and PCFG MAX/MIN ~0.35, which then collapse. Prepare for questions on these. p.9 says PCFG and universal-prior models 'fail on our ICL evaluations', while the Fig. 4 caption credits PCFG on assoc; quote the caption. Tasks (App. D): SUM = (x1+x2) mod 256 with x1, x2 != 0; STACK push = 250, pop = 251; ASSOC dictionary over bytes 1-255. [mine] The jagged PCFG curves suggest few instances. The tasks are close to the machine's own operations, so 'completely held-out tasks' (p.2) is plausible but untested.

slides.title: SUM: the model switches strategies in context
slides.content:
Task: [0, x1, x2, (x1 + x2) mod 256], x1, x2 != 0 (App. D); 1,024 trials; one learner, scale not stated
Entropy: of the next-byte distribution at the answer position, mean and IQR over trials (position is my inference; caption: "predictive entropy")
- m = 0: "preferred bytes" {0, 255, 1, 16}, "the marginally most common bytes" (p.11), ~92% of argmax; entropy ~7.6 bits
- After a few examples: copies context bytes, then "loses confidence"; entropy ~7.8 bits near m = 4-8 (uniform = 8)
- "After around 4 examples" it sums the low 4 bits; "by 8 examples" the high 4 bits too (p.11)
- m = 512: ~87% fully correct, but mean entropy still ~5 bits
Percentages, m ranges and entropy values are plot reads
slides.notes: Fig. 5, p.11. Paper's narrative (p.11): the prior, then copying previous bytes, then it 'loses confidence after several overconfident but incorrect predictions, reverting to a very broad distribution', then low bits after ~4 examples, high bits by 8, then it 'locks in on the correct approach'. Plot reads (left panel): m = 0 preferred ~92%, copy-context ~8%; m = 64 ~56% fully correct, with ~88% having the low 4 bits right; m = 512 ~87%. Right panel: ~6.9 bits at m = 64, ~5.05 at m = 512. [mine] Argmax is right by m = 512, but the distribution is still diffuse on a deterministic task; the paper does not discuss this. Speculative: 16 is a preferred byte, and macro X sets a cell to 16, so the prior may reflect the language, not natural data. The copy phase may depend on the prompt's byte format, which is untested.

slides.title: Pre-pretraining: warm start reaches each loss sooner
slides.content:
24.4M model: random init vs final self-play checkpoint, on DCLM, CIFAR-10, ESC-50 (App. A.1, p.21)
Natural-data tokens consumed to convergence, warm vs scratch (p.21):
- ESC-50: 320M vs 496M (-35%, my calc)
- CIFAR-10: 421M vs 588M (-28%, my calc)
- DCLM: no count in the text; Fig. 6 only
- Corpora ~255M / 146M / 152M tokens, repeated over epochs (A.2)
- Each arm tuned separately (LR x WD grid, 4 seeds per configuration); convergence = < 0.005 improvement for 5 evaluations, then a 200-step cosine decay (A.2)
- Gap "narrowed considerably" by the end (p.21); self-play compute not counted, "a one-time cost that amortizes" (p.22)
slides.notes: Figs. and text pp.21-22. Grids (A.2): LR in {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2}, WD in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.8}. Per arm, the configuration with the lowest mean converged BPB is kept. Caption: 'the warm start reaches every loss level first'. Open markers show the mean tokens consumed at convergence. Plot reads at 0 tokens (zero-shot): DCLM ~5.7 vs ~8.6, CIFAR-10 ~6.3 vs ~8.7, ESC-50 ~5.3 vs ~8.6. DCLM convergence markers read ~470M vs ~530M. Converged BPB is about 1.5-1.6 on DCLM and ~3.6-3.9 on CIFAR-10 and ESC-50 for both arms. The term 'pre-pretraining' is from Hu et al. 2025 (cited in A.1). [mine] One scale, and the claim is speed, not final loss. The 0-token DCLM warm start (~5.7) sits well above the Fig. 2 DCLM endpoint (~4.4). The paper does not reconcile them; possible reasons are a single model vs ensemble, checkpoint choice, or validation split. Do not put both on screen without saying so.

slides.title: Reward ablations: canonical best on 7 of 9 real datasets
slides.content:
1M learner; 4-seed ensembles; 256 held-out sequences per dataset; bits/byte (Table 5, p.31)
Columns: None = canonical Eq. 2 · uniform = generator removed, i.i.d. uniform programs · signed = no absolute value · shuffle = rewards permuted within the round's pool · last_step = window theta_{e-1} · loss_delta = realized loss change · negate = sign flipped
- Canonical best on 7 of 9 real datasets; the random-bytes row ties at 8.02 (uninformative)
- Signed wins on DCLM (5.06 vs 5.34) and C source (4.10 vs 4.16); the text says signed "does worse" (p.31)
- Shuffle: 0.2-1.2 bits worse than canonical, yet recovers 27-93% of the uniform-to-canonical gap (median 74%, my calc); paper: "much worse" (p.31)
- Negate: "worse than a randomly initialized model" (p.31), but Table 5 has no random-init row; audio 8-bit reads 7.67
- No variance shown; no row removes the preconditioner; last_step and loss_delta are bimodal across seeds
slides.notes: Table 5, p.31; exact values in the crop. Canonical wins outright on Metamath, DNA, arithmetic, audio 8-bit, audio 16-bit, melody (2.20 vs signed 2.21) and CIFAR planar. The caption says it 'often has lower variance as well', but no variance is shown. Footnotes: one loss_delta seed stopped at round 2587 and was excluded (3-seed ensemble). last_step and loss_delta are bimodal: DCLM last_step single seeds 6.4/6.5 vs 10.6/11.1; loss_delta 7.0 vs 9.8/12.3. Shuffle scope: the caption says 'across the program pool', the text 'between programs of the same batch'. [mine] The pool is the round's batch, so these likely mean the same. Shuffle shares over the nine rows: 27, 37, 61, 71, 74, 75, 78, 83, 93%. Uniform removes the generator, so the share measures what survives breaking the reward-program link, not the reward alone. Scale: Table 5 is 1M; Fig. 2 goes to ~25M, so do not compare numbers across them. Random-init reference: Fig. 6's from-scratch 0-token values are ~8.6-8.7.

slides.title: Pause: which result would you trust least?
slides.content:
Which result would you trust least?
Table 2 exponents · ICL (Fig. 4) · reward ablations (Table 5) · warm start (Fig. 6)
What single control would change your mind?
Unigram or copy-last-byte baseline on the same records · byte-permuted eval data · shuffled-reward run at scale
(Second click) The paper reports none of these three controls. Its trivial references are the 8.02 random-bytes row (Table 5) and the 3-bit DNA alphabet floor (App. B.5)
slides.notes: Discussion pause, about 1.5 minutes; no critique yet, it follows. Collect a show of hands on the first question, then one or two answers on the second. Then reveal the second-click line. Talking points from the paper's own setup: Table 2 compares exponents across tokenizers and models (p.21). Table 5 has no variance and no no-preconditioner row (p.31). ICL gives no model scale or instance counts (App. D). Fig. 6 excludes self-play compute (p.22). [mine] My own pick is the trivial baselines, which the critique section takes up first.

slides.title: Positioning: where this paper sits
slides.content:
Work | Natural data or pretrained model? | Adaptive generator? | Reward
Fixed synthetic distributions
Grau-Moya et al. 2024 | none: outputs of sampled UTM programs | no (fixed sampler) | none
Bloem 2025 | none: iterated random computation (p.13) | no | none
Hu et al. 2025 | formal languages, then natural language | no (hand-designed) | none
PCFG (Fig. 2 baseline) | none | no: random grammars from a fixed prior (App. H) | none
This paper
Self-play pretraining | none; both networks random init (p.4) | yes: RL + expert iteration | |preconditioned gradient alignment| since round floor(e/2) (Eq. 2)
Self-play from pretrained LLMs
Absolute Zero (Zhao 2025) | Qwen2.5-7B / 7B-Coder base | yes | learnability: 1 - solve rate, 0 if never solved; Python executor
LSP (Kuba 2025) | Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct | yes (Challenger) | LSP-Zero: zero-sum minimax; LSP adds a quality self-reward; task reward from Skywork-Reward-V2
G-Zero (Huang 2026) | Qwen3-8B-Base, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | yes (Proposer) | Hint-delta: how much a self-generated hint shifts the model's own log-probs; no verifier
UTM = universal Turing machine. The three LLM rows start from pretrained models, so they are not zero-data
slides.notes: Related Work (pp.13-14) calls Grau-Moya 2024 and Bloem 2025 'most relevant'; 'We instead learn the program distribution jointly with the learner' (p.14). Bloem 'provides evidence for universal pretraining from zero natural data' (p.13). Hu et al. 2025 is cited (pp.2, 13, 14, 21) but never run as a comparator. Cited: Absolute Zero (arXiv 2505.03335) and MINIMO (Poesia 2024), the one prior work the paper says starts from scratch (p.14). Not cited: LSP (2509.07414), G-Zero (2605.09959). Checked: AZR main runs use Qwen2.5-7B and 7B-Coder, Llama-3.1-8B only in extra runs; LSP full text: LSP-Zero is zero-sum, LSP adds self-reward, task reward from Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-3B. [interp] Avoid 'Absolute Zero, but for pretraining'. Nearest algorithmic cousin: Thrush et al. 2026 (RL generator, gradient-attribution reward, but toward a target). Their scores are reasoning benchmarks, not bits/byte.

slides.title: Strengths: what survives scrutiny
slides.content:
- Clean transfer test: no natural data in any gradient update (hyperparameters still selected on DCLM + DNA, p.8)
- Same program space, fixed sampler: the universal prior "scales substantially more slowly" (Fig. 2, p.7); DCLM endpoints ~6.9 vs self-play ~4.4 bpb (plot reads)
- Reward-only rows hurt (1M params, Table 5): DCLM negate 10.62, shuffle 5.96 vs canonical 5.34; uniform (7.75) removes the generator, not just the reward
- Four non-arithmetic families by round 512 (upper bound, 256-round resolution) vs > 53,000 rounds under the prior (95% bound from zero hits)
- Reports unflattering results: PCFG "stronger on text and code" (p.9); glibc rand flat at ~8 bits (Fig. 7)
slides.notes: About 1 minute; these were all shown in Results, so name them quickly. The figure is the Text (DCLM) and Python panels of Fig. 2. Point at DCLM: self-play ~4.4 at ~1e18, PCFG ~3.7 at ~4e17, universal prior ~6.9 (plot reads). The quotes are the paper's; calling them strengths is my reading. Signed beats canonical on DCLM and C (Table 5), so do not claim the absolute value helps on DCLM. Detail behind the families claim: App. C, 1.64e8 uniform samples with zero hits for the four families, at 1,024 programs per round. The warm-start result (Fig. 6) is a real but caveated strength: fewer natural-data tokens to convergence, a gap that 'narrowed considerably' (p.21), and self-play compute not counted (p.22).

slides.title: Limitations: the authors' and ours
slides.content:
Authors state
- "Initial proof-of-concept"; "models below 25M parameters at a 4K context" (pp.1, 15)
- Whether discovered math "causally contribute[s] to transfer" is untested (p.15)
- "Limited leakage through hyperparameter selection" on DCLM + DNA (p.8)
Our reading (calculations marked)
- No unigram, n-gram, PPM (prediction by partial matching) or copy-last-byte baseline; the only trivial rows are random bytes (8.02) and i.i.d. uniform programs (Table 5)
- Frontier points are picked by validation loss on the reported datasets; Table 2 gives b only, with no E, A, CIs or held-out extrapolation (pp.8, 21)
- Breaking the reward-program link keeps 74% of the DCLM gap (calc; 27-93% over 9 datasets, Table 5); mutation, replay, expert iteration and the archive are never ablated
slides.notes: Authors' wording: 'initial proof-of-concept' (Abstract); 'confined to models below 25M parameters at a 4K context' (p.15); 'we do not view universal pretraining as a replacement for natural data' (p.14); future work could test 'through circuit analysis or curriculum ablations' (p.15). More of ours, if time allows. DNA b = 0.435 vs 0.01-0.06; the paper already calls DNA 'the exceptional case' (p.8), and DNA is also a selection set. Metamath 0.129 and C 0.116 sit below 0.17 (the C value is derived, dagger). Self-play compute is excluded from the warm-start gains (p.22). Table 5 is a 1M model with 4 seeds and no error bars; loss_delta has 3 seeds; last_step and loss_delta are bimodal. [calc] Shuffle share: (7.75-5.96)/(7.75-5.34) = 74% on DCLM. Uniform removes the generator, so this is not a clean reward test. Grep of the paper: no n-gram, PPM, copy-last-byte or LPC baseline.

slides.title: What would convince us
slides.content:
1. Trivial baselines, same bits/byte and records: unigram, n-gram or PPM, copy-last-byte, LPC (linear predictive coding) for audio, hold/delta for melody
2. Shuffled-reward run at scale, plus separate ablations: mutation with and without the MAP-Elites archive (App. G), replay, expert iteration, KL term
3. Equal-compute comparison with formal-language pre-pretraining (Hu et al. 2025), with self-play compute counted
Next: held-out extrapolation of the fit (fit lower decades, predict the top); full compute accounting; ablate one discovered family from the curriculum
slides.notes: Item 1 is cheapest and most decisive; run it first. Item 2 targets reward vs pool: the Table 5 shuffle run keeps mutation, replay, expert iteration and KL. Item 3: per the Hu et al. 2025 abstract, a 1B model on ~1.6B natural tokens reaches the same loss with a 33% smaller token budget after formal-language pre-pretraining. This paper cites Hu et al. but never runs it. Next-line details. Fit: L(C) = E + A*C^-alpha per dataset (p.8), never tested out of sample. Compute: C = K x params x tokens (Fig. 1-2 axis labels; K is the seed count, p.8). Our reading is that it counts the learner only. Generator updates, program execution and the forward-mode JVP for Eq. 2 (pp.5-6, fn. 1) are not in C. Family ablation: our variant of the paper's suggested 'circuit analysis or curriculum ablations' (p.15). Selection hygiene also matters: tune on proxy data and report on untouched sets. [interp] Ask the room which item they would fund first.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.content:
Self-play zero-shot loss falls with compute on held-out natural data (paper's claim: Fig. 1, p.3; Fig. 2, p.7)
- Whether adaptivity causes the gap to the fixed prior is open (our reading): that comparison also removes the reward and the pool machinery
- Before trusting the exponents: trivial baselines, shuffle at scale, an equal-compute comparator
slides.notes: About 30 seconds. The paper's own summary (p.14): 'predictable improvements in next-token prediction on natural data can emerge even when no natural data is used for training.' Our reading: adaptivity is the proposed ingredient. But the fixed-prior comparison removes the reward, mutation, replay and expert iteration together, so it does not isolate adaptivity. Zero is strict for the two networks (random init, p.2), not for model selection (p.8); that is discussion question 4. Then move to the discussion slide.

slides.title: Discussion: two questions first
slides.content:
1. Is the learner learning universal structure, or marginals plus copying plus local smoothing? Which baseline would settle it?
2. On DCLM, shuffling keeps 74% of the gain over no generator (5.96 vs 7.75) but is 0.62 bpb worse than canonical (5.34). Is the reward or the pool doing the work?
Then:
3. What does self-play cost, counting generator updates, JVPs and program execution, next to the natural-data compute it replaces?
4. Paper, p.8: "natural data are never used for gradient updates." With DCLM + DNA model selection, is "zero data" the right label?
5. Music: is a 40-piece, absolute-pitch, hold-heavy melody benchmark measuring structure? Would warm starts help most for data-scarce symbolic music?
slides.notes: This slide stays up for the ~18-minute open discussion; take Q1 and Q2 first. Q1: the paper has no trivial baselines (limitations slide). Q2: both readings are true; the paper calls shuffle 'much worse' (p.31) against canonical, while against no generator it keeps most of the gain. Also ask whether shuffle permutes across the pool (caption) or within a batch (text, p.31). Q3: C has no generator or JVP term (Fig. 1 axis). Q4: put the p.8 sentence on screen before asking. Q5 is my angle: Mutopia is 40 hand-picked pieces, absolute pitch with no transposition invariance, one byte per 16th note so 'hold' dominates (B.4). Per-onset entropy or event-based MIDI tokens would test it better. Spares: why does a random PCFG beat self-play on text and code (p.9), and would a PCFG plus self-play mixture beat both? Do LSP and G-Zero belong in the comparison, given they start from pretrained models?

sections.name: Hook and background
sections.description: 5 slides, about 5 minutes: title, the curated-data hook with the paper's test and scope, a one-line roadmap, Solomonoff induction as background (with the paper's g_0 prior), and self-play as an adaptive search that rejects a difficulty reward. The program language moved to Method to avoid duplication.

sections.name: Method
sections.description: 7 slides, about 11 minutes: the self-play loop, the Brainf*ck-plus-macros language, generator and learner objectives (Eqs. 1, 3-5), the reward (Eq. 2), one reconstructed round with what the paper leaves unreported, compute and selection on the scaling axis, and a 1.5-minute question pause. Table 5 numbers are deferred to Results.

sections.name: Evaluation and results
sections.description: 10 slides, about 17 minutes: zero-shot byte encodings and floors, Fig. 2 scaling against two fixed priors, Table 2 exponents, discovered math families (Table 1), later generator checkpoints (Fig. 3), ICL (Fig. 4) and the SUM strategy shift (Fig. 5), pre-pretraining (Fig. 6), reward ablations (Table 5), and a 1.5-minute pause.

sections.name: Positioning, critique and discussion
sections.description: 6 slides, about 7 minutes, then about 18 minutes of open discussion: positioning against fixed-distribution and pretrained-LLM self-play work, strengths, limitations (authors' and ours), what would convince us, takeaways, and the discussion slide that stays up for the open discussion.
